title: Cesar Chavez Fasts for Nonviolence
text:
By early 1968 the grape strike led by Cesar Chavez and the United Farm Workers in Delano, California, had dragged on for more than two years. Growers were hiring strikebreakers, and some strikers had grown frustrated and were talking about violence. There had been incidents of sabotage and threats.

In February 1968 Chavez stopped eating. He announced the fast to union members as an act of penance and a call to recommit to nonviolence, not as a hunger strike against the growers. He moved to a small room at the union's headquarters near Delano, and farm workers began coming there every day for mass and to visit him.

The fast lasted twenty-five days. Chavez lost a great deal of weight and his health suffered. On March 10, 1968, he broke the fast at a mass in a Delano park with thousands of farm workers. Senator Robert F. Kennedy came to share bread with him. Chavez was too weak to speak, and a statement was read for him saying that the truest act of courage was to sacrifice oneself for others in a totally nonviolent struggle for justice.

The movement stayed nonviolent. In 1970 most table grape growers signed union contracts.
lesson: To change how your followers act, you may need to show it in your own body first. Personal sacrifice can carry a message no order can.
source: Contemporary press reports; United Farm Workers records; Chavez's statement of March 10, 1968
